title: Work efficiently and reproducibly
goal: Read less data, combine chunk summaries correctly, and make repeatable samples.
prerequisites: Understand grouping, CSV I/O, and data types.

cells.title: Measure memory use
cells.explanation: memory_usage(deep=True) estimates memory including text stored by object columns. Repeated labels may use less memory as categories. The benefit depends on the data, so measure it instead of assuming.
cells.code:
labels = pd.Series(["RAK", "Dubai"] * 500, dtype=object)
category = labels.astype("category")
result = pd.Series({"Object_bytes": labels.memory_usage(deep=True), "Category_bytes": category.memory_usage(deep=True)})
print(result)

questions.prompt: Why repeat only two labels many times?
questions.answer: It demonstrates data with few unique text values and many repeated occurrences.

questions.prompt: Will converting to category change the label values?
questions.answer: No. It changes their representation, not the label meanings.

questions.prompt: Are exact byte counts guaranteed on every computer?
questions.answer: No. They depend on versions and storage details; compare the measurements in your environment.

cells.task: Measure 1,000 unique text labels before and after category conversion. Explain why the saving may shrink or disappear.
cells.solution:
labels = pd.Series([f"ID_{i}" for i in range(1000)], dtype=object)
category = labels.astype("category")
result = pd.Series({"Object_bytes": labels.memory_usage(deep=True), "Category_bytes": category.memory_usage(deep=True)})
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Categories also store the distinct labels and codes. With nearly every label unique, that overhead can outweigh any benefit.

check.prompt: When is category often useful for memory?
options: Many repeated values from a small set
Only when the column is numeric
check.feedback: A small category dictionary can represent many repeated labels compactly.

cells.watch: This is a small storage demonstration, not a benchmark of all pandas workloads.
cells.takeaway: Choose data types based on meaning and measurement.

cells.title: Load only needed columns
cells.explanation: usecols avoids reading columns that the question does not need. Explicit dtypes make the import contract clearer. This small file demonstrates a habit that becomes useful with larger files.
cells.code:
result = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Student_ID", "Program", "Score"], dtype={"Student_ID": "string", "Program": "category"})
print(result.head())
print(result.dtypes)

questions.prompt: Which six source columns are omitted?
questions.answer: Name, Campus, Age, Study_Hours, Attendance, and Join_Date.
All 12 rows; usecols limits columns, not rows.

questions.prompt: Why not load every field just in case?
questions.answer: Unneeded columns use memory and add distractions to the analysis.

cells.task: Read only Student_ID and Attendance, and limit the preview to the first four file rows with nrows.
cells.solution:
result = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Student_ID", "Attendance"], nrows=4, dtype={"Student_ID": "string"})
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Only four rows and two columns are loaded. This preview does not represent the whole dataset.

options: Loads only the first four data rows
check.feedback: nrows limits the number of parsed data rows from the beginning of the file.

cells.watch: A file preview can miss problems that occur later in the file.
cells.takeaway: Read the fields and rows needed for the current step.

cells.title: Combine chunk totals correctly
cells.explanation: chunksize reads a CSV in pieces. A total and a non-missing count can be accumulated across pieces without keeping all rows. Divide the overall total by the overall count to calculate the overall mean.
cells.code:
total = 0
count = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Score"], chunksize=5):
    total += chunk["Score"].sum()
    count += chunk["Score"].count()
result = total / count
print("Known scores:", count)
print("Mean score:", round(result, 2))

questions.prompt: What is chunk in each loop iteration?
questions.answer: A DataFrame containing the next group of file rows, up to five rows here.

questions.prompt: Why not average the three chunk means equally?
questions.answer: The chunks have different counts; equal weighting would give the two-row chunk too much influence.

cells.task: Use chunks of four rows and calculate how many students score at least 80 without retaining all rows.
cells.hint: Add the sum of a Boolean condition for each chunk.
cells.solution:
result = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Score"], chunksize=4):
    result += chunk["Score"].ge(80).sum()
print("Students with Score >= 80:", result)
cells.solution_note: Six students meet the threshold, regardless of the chosen chunk boundaries.

check.prompt: What is needed for an exact combined mean?
options: An unweighted mean of chunk means
A combined sum and non-missing count
check.feedback: The overall mean is the total of known values divided by their total count.

cells.watch: Not every operation is easy to compute in chunks. A global sort or median needs a different strategy.
cells.takeaway: Combine summaries using their correct mathematical weights.

cells.title: Take a repeatable sample
cells.explanation: sample chooses rows randomly. random_state makes the selection repeatable for this data and environment. Reproducibility does not make a tiny sample representative of the population.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df.sample(n=3, random_state=7)
repeat = df.sample(n=3, random_state=7)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Campus", "Score"]])
print("Same sample:", result.equals(repeat))

questions.prompt: Will the repeated call with the same input and seed match?
questions.answer: Yes, within the same sampling environment.

questions.prompt: Does a fixed seed remove sampling bias?
questions.answer: No. It makes the selection reproducible; it does not guarantee a balanced or representative sample.

cells.task: Take two students from each campus using groupby.sample with random_state=7.
cells.hint: Group by Campus before calling sample(n=2, random_state=7).
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df.groupby("Campus", group_keys=False).sample(n=2, random_state=7)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Campus", "Score"]])
print(result["Campus"].value_counts())
cells.solution_note: The result has four students, two from each campus. Equal counts here are a chosen design, not a universal sampling rule.

check.prompt: What does a seed mainly provide?
check.feedback: A seed controls the random sequence; it does not establish statistical validity.

cells.watch: Document input data, row order, library versions, and seed when an exact sample matters.
cells.takeaway: Repeatability and representativeness are different goals.
